title: India Almost Missed the World Cup Entirely. Not as a Team. As a Country That Could Watch It.
excerpt: Zee's last-minute FIFA deal, the Unite8 Sports launch, and where NRIs in the US, UK, and Canada can stream every match for free
body:
For months, India was an embarrassment on the global football calendar. The FIFA World Cup 2026 — the biggest in history, 48 teams, 104 matches across three countries — was ten days from kickoff. And the world's second-most-populous nation had no broadcaster.

China had signed a deal on May 15. Japan, Indonesia, Singapore, and Hong Kong were locked in. In India, nothing. FIFA's official line was that discussions "are ongoing and must remain confidential." Delhi High Court issued notices to Prasar Bharati after a citizen petition demanded Doordarshan carry the tournament free-to-air. An obscure Washington DC firm called Avni LLC claimed to have won the India rights through a $300 million bid.

Then, on June 1, Zee Entertainment ended the circus.

The Deal

Zee has signed an eight-year agreement with FIFA covering 39 events from 2026 through 2034. This is not a one-tournament deal. It includes the 2026 FIFA World Cup, the 2030 World Cup, the 2027 Women's World Cup, and multiple youth and futsal tournaments. Reports suggest FIFA initially sought $100 million for the Indian subcontinent package before settling at approximately $60 million — a steep discount that reflects how late the negotiations went and how few alternatives FIFA had.

For Zee, this marks a re-entry into sports broadcasting roughly eight years after selling its sports assets to Sony. The company is backing the deal with a new brand: Unite8 Sports.

Following the announcement, Zee's stock rose approximately 7 percent.

How to Watch in India

The 2026 World Cup will be broadcast on four new linear channels:

  • Unite8 Sports 1 (Hindi) — ₹7/month
  • Unite8 Sports 1 HD (Hindi) — ₹9/month
  • Unite8 Sports 2 (English) — ₹8/month
  • Unite8 Sports 2 HD (English) — ₹11/month

Digital streaming will be available on ZEE5. Subscription tiers range from a free ad-supported plan (likely with delayed or limited access) to premium plans at ₹299/quarter and ₹599/year.

The first match kicks off on June 11 in Mexico City: South Africa vs Mexico. The tournament runs until July 19, with the final at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey.

How NRIs Can Watch From Abroad

For the Indian diaspora in North America, the situation is simpler — and free.

United States and Canada: All 104 matches will be available on Willow Sports across major FAST (free ad-supported streaming) platforms. Willow TV, Willow TV Canada, and Cricbuzz partnerships will carry additional coverage. No subscription required.

United Kingdom: Coverage details for UK-based NRIs will be available through ITV and the BBC, which have shared the rights. Every match will be free-to-air.

Australia: SBS will broadcast select matches free-to-air, with Stan Sport carrying the full tournament on streaming.

ZEE5's global availability may also provide an option for diaspora viewers, though geo-restrictions and rights windows could limit access in markets where other broadcasters hold exclusivity.

Why It Took So Long

The deadlock was a story of mismatched ambitions. FIFA's initial valuation of the Indian rights was pegged at around $100 million — a figure that made sense on paper given India's 1.4 billion population and growing football interest, but one that Indian broadcasters considered wildly inflated given the sport's relatively modest television ratings compared to cricket.

The JioStar combine (the merged entity of Viacom18 and Star India) was the expected frontrunner, having carried the 2022 World Cup on JioCinema and Sports18. But negotiations stalled over valuation. Neither JioStar nor Sony showed willingness to meet FIFA's asking price.

That left Zee, which had been largely absent from sports since selling TEN Sports to Sony in 2018. The company's decision to build Unite8 Sports from scratch — four channels, a digital platform, Hindi and English commentary — suggests this is not a one-off gamble but a strategic bet on football as a long-term property in India.

What the Avni LLC Episode Revealed

Before Zee's deal was confirmed, Avni LLC — a Washington DC-based Indian-American investment firm led by Deelip Mhaske — claimed publicly that an associated partner had secured the winning bid for India. The company pitched a vision built on OTT platforms, AI-powered multilingual broadcasting, and mobile micro-subscriptions.

FIFA never confirmed Avni LLC's claim. The episode revealed the chaos surrounding the Indian market and the level of opportunism the vacuum attracted.

The Bigger Picture for Indian Football

India is not at this World Cup. The men's national team remains ranked outside the top 100 by FIFA. But four players with Indian roots — Sarpreet Singh (New Zealand), Tahsin Ibrahim Tijani (Nigeria), Jean-Philippe Velupillay (Canada), and Stéphane Moutoussamy (France's squad contender) — will be in the tournament.

Football viewership in India has grown steadily, driven by the Indian Super League, the Premier League's popularity among urban audiences, and the cultural reach of Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo. The 2022 World Cup final between Argentina and France drew an estimated 100 million viewers in India.

Zee's bet is that the 2026 edition — stretched across North American time zones that are friendlier for Indian evening viewing than Qatar was — will build on that momentum. The matches start as early as 9:30 PM IST and run through the night, fitting neatly into the late-night viewing habits of young Indian audiences.

For NRIs in the US, the timing is even better: afternoon and evening kickoffs across Eastern and Pacific time. For the first time, the diaspora can watch the World Cup in their adopted country's stadiums and on their home country's broadcast simultaneously.

The biggest tournament in football history starts in three days. India, finally, has a way to watch it.
